phrasing.text: In plain words: the police or anyone else may not arrest a relative, friend or any other person in place of the suspect they are looking for, for example to pressure the suspect to come forward.

In plain words: how the Nigeria Police Force is funded, through its General Fund, budget allocations and other money paid to the Force.

In plain words: it is an offence for a data controller or data processor to disobey a compliance order of the Data Protection Commission; the punishment is a fine of up to the higher or standard maximum amount, up to one year in prison, or both.
In plain words: this Act overrides any other law that is inconsistent with it on the processing of personal data; where they conflict, the Data Protection Act takes priority.

In plain words: a child may not be discriminated against because of community, ethnic group, place of origin, sex, religion or political opinion, and may not be disadvantaged because of the circumstances of his or her birth, for example being born outside marriage.
In plain words: no parent, guardian or anyone else may promise or engage a child in marriage to anyone (child betrothal); such a promise is void.

In plain words: who may adopt a child: a married couple who are both at least 25 and authorised to adopt jointly, a married person with the spouse's consent, or a single person aged at least 35 adopting a child of the same sex; every adopter must be found suitable by the investigating officers.

In plain words: compensation for a work injury or death cannot be signed over, charged, seized or attached by a creditor, and passes only to a personal representative; nothing may be deducted from it except government welfare assistance advanced to the person or money owed to the Board.

In plain words: if a person cannot read or write, the Board may excuse them from giving written notice under the Act, such as notice of an injury or claim, and accept notice in any form it considers appropriate.

In plain words: the kinds of works copyright can protect in Nigeria are literary works, musical works, artistic works, audiovisual works, sound recordings and broadcasts; a literary, musical or artistic work must show some original effort and be fixed in a medium, whatever its quality or purpose.
In plain words: you do not need to register a work or complete any formality for it to be protected by copyright.

In plain words: Nigerian folklore is protected by copyright law against reproduction, public performance or broadcast, and adaptation or translation for commercial use or outside its traditional context, with exceptions such as private use and education; the source community must be acknowledged, and the Commission controls the right to authorise these uses.

In plain words: where a person's income cannot be worked out, or proper records are not kept, for example a small trader without books, the person is taxed under a presumptive tax regime on terms set by the Minister in regulations, on the advice of the Joint Revenue Board.

In plain words: the businesses that can get the economic development tax incentive are those in the priority sectors listed in the Tenth Schedule, which also sets how long the incentive lasts; the President may direct changes to the list.

In plain words: the punishment for murder is the death sentence. A person who was under seventeen at the time of the offence is not sentenced to death but is detained during the pleasure of the President. A woman convicted of murder who says she is pregnant goes through a set procedure first.

In plain words: a person who buys, accepts or keeps something knowing it was stolen or obtained by crime commits the felony of receiving stolen property. It can carry fourteen years in prison, or seven years where the thing came from a misdemeanor.
In plain words: this is the right of private defence, also called self-defence. Doing something in the lawful exercise of that right is not an offence.

In plain words: this is the insanity defence. A person is not guilty if, because of unsoundness of mind, they could not know the nature of what they were doing or that it was wrong or against the law.

In plain words: this is the offence of bigamy, marrying again while a husband or wife is still alive. It does not apply where the earlier marriage was legally dissolved, or where the other spouse has been absent and unheard of for seven years and the new partner is told the facts.
